findings.title: SHA-256 message-length bound uses LessEqThan on an unconstrained field input, allowing a near-p/negative length and an all-zero hash
findings.evidence: In Sha256General the only upper bound on the attacker-supplied SHA-256 message length is `component bitLengthVerifier = LessEqThan(maxBitsPaddedBits); bitLengthVerifier.in[0] <== paddedInLength; bitLengthVerifier.in[1] <== maxBitLength; bitLengthVerifier.out === 1;` (lines 125-128; identical block at 237-240 in Sha256Partial). `paddedInLength` is a free field element and is never range-checked with Num2Bits, but circomlib's LessThan/LessEqThan is only a sound integer comparator when both operands fit in `maxBitsPaddedBits` bits: it enforces range only through `n2b.in <== in[0] + (1<<n) - in[1]` and the sign bit of the resulting (n+1)-bit decomposition. A malicious prover can therefore choose `paddedInLength` equal to a small negative representative modulo the BN254 prime p (e.g. p-k), so the modular sum wraps to a small value and `bitLengthVerifier.out === 1` is satisfied for an out-of-range/negative length. Because `inBlockIndex` is tied to the length only by the field equation `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` (line 111/234), which is satisfiable for any length via field division, this is the only length check and it is bypassable. The derived selector index `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1` (line 196) is then a large near-p value that also defeats ItemAtIndex's `LessThan(bitLength)` bound (array.circom lines 25-28), so no `eqs[i]` matches and every `out[k]` is forced to 0. The prover thus produces a valid proof that the all-zero 256-bit value is the SHA-256 digest of an arbitrary/malformed message, breaking soundness for any consumer of Sha256General/Sha256Bytes (e.g. commitment schemes). Reachability: fully attacker-controlled witness inputs `paddedIn`, `paddedInLength` to Sha256Bytes/Sha256General; no external precondition beyond the ability to generate a proof.
